Q: Bit numbering and endianness A:

Short answer: correct, endianness does NOT concern itself with the order of bits within a byte - only the order of bytes within a greater structure.

Q: C# Socket handling - how to set the timeout A:

Yeah, this isn't great code at all. I'm going to hazard that synchronous Send and Receive are being used, which should anyway be converted to async calls. Async calls are given their own cancellation tokens, you don't set it on the socket directly.

_socket.SetSocketOption( SocketOptionLevel.Socket, SocketOptionName.SendTimeout, timeout );

This is the same as calling:

_socket.SendTimeout = 1000;

lower down, so these two calls are conflicting. The latter notes in the docs: "This option applies to synchronous Send calls only." You should be using asynchronous code anyway.

_socket.Blocking = true;

Again "The Blocking property has no effect on asynchronous methods" so it doesn't do anything in that case. Even in synchronous mode, TCP sockets will block either way.

_socket.SendBufferSize = 8192;

Why mess with this? Windows can allocate dynamic buffers much better than you can.

_socket.LingerState = new LingerOption( true, 10 );

The default behaviour is :

Graceful shutdown, immediate return — allowing the shutdown sequence to complete in the background. Although this is the default behavior, the application has no way of knowing when (or whether) the graceful shutdown sequence actually completes.

In most cases it shouldn't be necessary to set a Linger option.

Q: describe any issues which might prevent the PC code from running on the 8-bit system A:

Code written for a 64-bit PC may not run correctly on an 8-bit embedded processor due to several issues:

   Data size differences: Types such as int, long, and pointers are larger on a 64-bit system, which may cause overflow or incorrect memory usage on an 8-bit system.

   Memory constraints: Embedded systems have very limited RAM and storage, so code designed for a PC may be too large.

   Alignment and architecture differences: The CPU architecture (instruction set, endianness, alignment requirements) may differ, causing incompatibility.

   Performance limitations: 8-bit processors are much slower and may not handle complex operations efficiently.

   Missing OS features: Embedded systems may lack features like full OS support, threads, or system calls used in PC code.

Q: Python Get Request URL returning errors compared to hard-coded URL A:

Your current code works correctly.

But error shows problem with response_ROC = requests.get(request_ROC)
which I don't see it in current code. It seems you got it in original version.

But if you try print(request_ROC) then you get <Response [200]> so it can run

response_ROC = requests.get("<Response [200]>")

and this can make problem.

Or maybe you simply forgot .url in original code.

response_ROC = requests.get(request_ROC.url)

and now it works correctly.

Q: Apparently my code is AI generated (Except it's not) A:

I was getting comments such as: "too clean and too organized," "consistent naming conventions", "direct comments explaining the code"

I had to laugh at this. What happens when AI produces clean, well-organized code with consistent naming conventions?

Missing. F*****g. Accomplished.

In all seriousness, though, try removing comments that explain the code and run it through the tool again. Some related Software Engineering questions:

  • What's wrong with comments that explain complex code?
  • Coding standard for clarity: comment every line of code?

Q: What is "crypt key missing" error in Pgadmin4 and how to resolve it? A:

Bug is still present in pgAdmin 9.14

On initial run, even if you set a master password it doesn't work and any server connection you make is permanently tainted and will never accept a password, so you get "Crypt key missing" and "no password supplied" errors.

You have to quit, reset the master password, then create a new server connection entry, and only then will the password be actually passed to the server (and can be saved).
